acknowledgment.title: A place of First Peoples
paragraphs: The islands and waters of this journey are the homelands of Coast Salish peoples, who have lived on, fished, travelled and cared for them since time immemorial — and still do.
Among them are the Lummi, Samish, Swinomish, Songhees and W̱SÁNEĆ peoples, and other Nations whose ties to these islands reach across today’s border.
You paddle here as a guest. Travel lightly, and listen.
acknowledgment.note: Draft — to be reviewed with the Nations named before public release.

safetyNote.title: Before you paddle
paragraphs: Salish Sea Expeditions teaches real sea-kayaking skills, but a game is not a substitute for instruction and practice on the water.
Learn rescues with a qualified instructor, paddle with others, check real tide and current predictions, and dress for immersion.
The chart in this game is simplified. Do not use it for navigation.

layers.name: Base layer
layers.text: Wool or synthetic, next to the skin. It moves sweat away so you stay dry inside everything else. Cotton holds water and stops insulating — leave it at home.

layers.name: Insulating layer
layers.text: Fleece top and bottoms, chosen for the water, not the air. The Salish Sea is about 8 °C in winter and only 10–12 °C in summer — dress for a swim whenever it is below about 21 °C.

layers.name: Drysuit
layers.text: A waterproof, breathable shell with latex gaskets at the neck and wrists and built-in socks. It keeps the water out; the layers underneath keep you warm. Crouch and let the trapped air out before you close the zip.

layers.name: Spray skirt & PFD
layers.text: The skirt seals you into the cockpit — grab loop outside, always. The PFD goes on last and stays on: a whistle on its cord, a blunt-tipped rescue knife, the VHF in a pocket.

layers.name: Head, hands & feet
layers.text: A neoprene cap, gloves or pogies, and booties. Head and hands lose warmth fast, and booties save your feet from barnacles and oyster shell when you land. Sunglasses for the glare off the water.

kitGroups.name: On you
kitGroups.text: Worn, or clipped to your PFD — it has to come with you if the boat does not.

kitGroups.name: On deck
kitGroups.text: Under the deck lines, where you can reach it without opening anything.

kitGroups.name: Inside the boat
kitGroups.text: In dry bags, loaded through the cockpit — this kayak has no hatches.

kit.name: PFD
kit.text: Worn every minute on the water, zipped and snug. It only works if you have it on.

kit.name: Whistle
kit.text: Required in both countries. Carries farther than a shout and never loses its voice.

kit.name: Rescue knife
kit.text: Blunt-tipped, on the PFD, for a tangled line. Reachable with either hand.

kit.name: VHF radio
kit.text: On you, not in the boat. Channel 16 reaches the Coast Guard and the ferries; you can hear traffic before you see it.

kit.name: Light
kit.text: Camp after sunset — and the white light the rules ask you to have ready if you are on the water after dark.

kit.name: Bilge pump
kit.text: After a re-entry the cockpit is full of water. Required in Canada (a pump or a bailer).

kit.name: Paddle float
kit.text: Turns your paddle into an outrigger so you can climb back in alone.

kit.name: Throw bag, 15 m
kit.text: A buoyant heaving line. Required in Canadian waters — you will cross into them.

kit.name: Tow line
kit.text: On a quick-release belt. For a tired partner, or a boat that has lost its paddler.

kit.name: Chart & compass
kit.text: In a clear case on the deck in front of you. The phone is a backup, not the plan.

kit.name: Spare paddle
kit.text: In two halves under the deck lines. Paddles do get dropped.

kit.name: Tent
kit.text: Poles out of the bag and packed flat: long, thin things fit a folding kayak best.

kit.name: Sleeping bag & pad
kit.text: In your driest bag. A wet sleeping bag makes a cold night colder.

kit.name: Food & stove
kit.text: Food in a hard canister: Jones Island’s raccoons open zips.

kit.name: Water, 8 L
kit.text: Jones Island’s tap normally runs May to September, but it is off until further notice. Carry it all.

kit.name: Camp clothes
kit.text: Dry clothes that never touch the sea: a warm layer, a hat, dry socks.

kit.name: First-aid kit
kit.text: Blisters, cuts, and the day you need more — plus a way to call for help.

items: A wearable life jacket (PFD) for each person
A white light — a torch will do — ready to show from sunset to sunrise and in fog
A PFD or lifejacket for each person
A light, if out after dark or in fog

gear.name: Tent
gear.text: A night out needs a roof.

gear.name: Sleeping bag & pad
gear.text: Keep it in the driest bag you have.

gear.name: Water, 8 L
gear.text: Jones Island’s tap normally runs May to September, but it has been off until further notice — carry all your water. Heavy: pack it low and central.

gear.name: Food & stove
gear.text: Pack it in a hard canister; raccoons are waiting.

gear.name: Warm layers
gear.text: Even in July, the Salish Sea is about 10–12 °C.

gear.name: First-aid kit
gear.text: Blisters, cuts, and the day you need more.

gear.name: Bilge pump
gear.text: Clip it on deck: after a re-entry you need it immediately.

gear.name: Paddle float
gear.text: Makes solo re-entry far easier. Keep it on deck, within reach.

gear.name: Spare paddle
gear.text: Split paddle under the deck lines.

gear.name: VHF radio
gear.text: Channel 16 for emergencies; you can hear ferry traffic too.

gear.name: Headlamp
gear.text: Camp chores after sunset, and a light to be seen by.

gear.name: Chart & compass
gear.text: In a clear bag on the deck, where you can read it.

kayakParts.name: Bow
kayakParts.text: The front of the kayak. It rises to meet waves and carries the front flotation bag.

kayakParts.name: Stern
kayakParts.text: The back of the kayak. The stern flotation bag and heavier dry bags ride here.

kayakParts.name: Deck
kayakParts.text: The top of the boat. Deck lines give you and your partner something to grab in a rescue.

kayakParts.name: Hull
kayakParts.text: The underside, in the water. Its shape decides how the boat tracks, turns and feels on edge. The hull is white below a black perimeter line, so an upturned boat is easy to spot.

kayakParts.name: Keel
kayakParts.text: The spine along the bottom. It helps the boat run straight.

kayakParts.name: Chine
kayakParts.text: Where the side of the hull turns under. Tilting onto the chine — edging — is how you carve a turn.

kayakParts.name: Cockpit & coaming
kayakParts.text: Where you sit. The raised rim, the coaming, is what the spray skirt seals around. On this folding kayak, gear also loads through the cockpit — there are no hatches.

kayakParts.name: Spray skirt
kayakParts.text: A neoprene or nylon deck you wear. It seals you in so waves stay out. Always leave the grab loop outside — it is how you release it in a wet exit.

kayakParts.name: Frame & skin
kayakParts.text: An aluminium frame inside a tough waterproof skin — a modern descendant of the skin-on-frame kayaks of Arctic peoples. The tubes are colour-coded, blue forward of the cockpit and red aft, around carbon ribs, so it goes together the same way every time. The whole boat packs into one wheeled bag about 104 cm tall and 24 kg — small enough to walk onto a ferry.

kayakParts.name: Hull jacks
kayakParts.text: Three jacks — one along each side, one on the keel — tension the skin and set the rocker. Less rocker tracks straight on a crossing; more rocker turns quickly among rocks. You can adjust them while paddling.

kayakParts.name: Flotation bags
kayakParts.text: Dry bags fore and aft that hold your gear and keep the kayak afloat if you capsize. A half-empty boat without them would fill with water.

bodyPoints.name: Feet on the pegs
bodyPoints.text: Balls of the feet on the foot pegs, toes relaxed. Each stroke pushes through the foot on the stroke side.

bodyPoints.name: Knees in the thigh braces
bodyPoints.text: Knees up and out, pressing lightly into the thigh braces. This is your steering wheel — lift a knee and the boat tilts.

bodyPoints.name: Hips connect you
bodyPoints.text: You wear a kayak, you do not sit in it. The hips carry the connection from the body to the boat: lower body steers and tilts, upper body drives.

bodyPoints.name: Backband at the pelvis
bodyPoints.text: The backband supports the pelvis, not the shoulders. Sit tall, slightly forward — never slumped against it.

bodyPoints.name: Head over the boat
bodyPoints.text: Keep your head over the kayak. The body follows the head: lift it too early in a brace or roll and you go over.

paddleParts.name: Blade
paddleParts.text: Long, narrow and unfeathered: the Greenland paddle is the Arctic original. A narrow blade enters quietly and buries fully, so it pulls with the whole torso rather than yanking the shoulders.

paddleParts.name: Loom
paddleParts.text: The short centre shaft. Hold it with your hands at its shoulders, knuckles up, thumbs and forefingers lightly around the blade roots — a loose grip you can feel the water through.

paddleParts.name: Shoulders
paddleParts.text: Where the loom widens into the blade. Your hands rest against them, so you always know where the blade is without looking, and the paddle can slide out along the blade for a long, extended stroke or roll.

paddleParts.name: Tip & cant
paddleParts.text: The blade goes in angled slightly forward (canted), so it slices in cleanly and holds the water as it moves back. Cedar, carved to the paddler’s own arm span — the oldest kind of custom fit.

paddleParts.name: The paddler’s box
paddleParts.text: Keep your hands in front of your chest, in the box formed by your arms and shoulders. It protects your shoulders and keeps the power in your torso.

drills.title: Forward stroke: rotate, don’t pull
drills.text: Wind up your torso, plant the blade by your feet and unwind. Your arms stay nearly straight; the stroke ends at your hip. Hold the water and let the strokes come at a rhythm; a tap is an arm stroke.

drills.title: Reverse stroke: look back, push
drills.text: Rotate to look over your shoulder, plant the back of the blade behind your hip and push it forward to your feet. The same torso, the other way. Slide your thumb up while holding.

drills.title: Edging: lift a knee
drills.text: Lift one knee to tilt the kayak onto its chine, keeping your head and body over the boat. Drag the hips strip toward the side you want to go down.
drills.goal: Hold an edge for three seconds

drills.title: Turning: the sweep stroke
drills.text: A wide arc from bow to stern turns the boat away from the blade: sweep on the left to turn right. Edge toward the sweep side and it turns far more. Lean to steer while you paddle, or flick sideways for a single sweep.
drills.goal: Turn half a circle with edged sweeps
drills.keys: A or D while holding W; Z or C for one sweep; Q or E to edge

drills.title: Low brace and hip snap
drills.text: When you tip, slap the back of the blade flat on the water on the low side, then snap your hips to bring the boat back under you. Head stays down — it comes up last.

drills.title: Wet exit and paddle-float re-entry
drills.text: The last drill is the one you hope never to need. Go over on purpose, here in the harbour: out of the boat, the paddle float on one blade as an outrigger, up onto the back deck and in, then pump dry. Do it once in calm water and the real one is a thing you have done before.
drills.goal: Out, back in, and pumped dry
drills.keys: the boat goes over on its own — read each card

places.name: Anacortes ferry terminal
places.text: Washington State Ferries leave Anacortes for the San Juan Islands. A folding kayak rides aboard as walk-on luggage — no car, no roof rack.

places.name: Friday Harbor
places.text: The islands’ largest town and ferry landing on San Juan Island: a working harbour of fishing boats, sailboats, kayak outfitters and a busy summer waterfront.

places.name: Friday Harbor Laboratories
places.text: The University of Washington’s marine research station, just north of town. Scientists have studied the rich waters of the San Juans here for over a century.

places.name: Shaw Island
places.text: The smallest of the ferry-served islands, quiet and wooded, across the channel from Friday Harbor.

places.name: Yellow Island
places.text: A tiny island protected as a nature preserve, famous for spring wildflowers.

places.name: Lopez Island
places.text: The flattest and most farmed of the big islands, which is why cyclists love it. The ferry passes its north shore after Thatcher Pass; Upright Head is the point with the ferry landing.

places.name: Thatcher Pass
places.text: The gap between Blakely Island to the north and Decatur Island to the south: the door from Rosario Strait into the inner islands. Every Anacortes ferry threads it.

places.name: Orcas Island
places.text: The largest and highest of the islands, shaped like a horseshoe around East Sound. Mount Constitution, 732 m, is the high point of the whole archipelago; the ferry passes under its southern shore in Harney Channel.

places.name: Wasp Passage
places.text: The narrow run between Shaw Island and Crane Island, with the Wasp Islands scattered to the north. Strong currents and small boats: the ferry slows here.

places.name: San Juan Island
places.text: Home to Friday Harbor, the Lime Kiln whale-watching shore and the old English and American camps. San Juan Channel runs along its east side, and the ferry turns down it for the landing.

places.name: Jones Island Marine State Park
places.text: A small island park reachable only by water, with paddle-in campsites on the Cascadia Marine Trail — and famously bold raccoons.

places.name: Spieden Island
places.text: A long private island, grass on its south face and forest on its north, that walls the north side of Spieden Channel. There is no landing.

places.name: Spieden Channel
places.text: The run between Spieden Island and the north shore of San Juan Island, from San Juan Channel west to Haro Strait. Strong currents, and rips off the points.

places.name: Davison Head
places.text: The headland on the north of San Juan Island where Spieden Channel opens to Haro Strait, with Roche Harbor behind it.

places.name: Posey Island Marine State Park
places.text: A one-acre island at the mouth of Roche Harbor, reached only by small boat, with two primitive campsites on the Cascadia Marine Trail and no drinking water.

places.name: Roche Harbor
places.text: A resort harbour and port of entry on the north-west of San Juan Island, once the largest lime works on the west coast.

lessons.title: You wear a kayak
lessons.text: Feet on the pegs, knees in the braces, backband at the pelvis. The better the fit, the more your hips can do.

lessons.title: Power comes from the torso
lessons.text: Arms tire in minutes; the torso and legs can paddle all day. A rotation stroke moves the boat further for less effort.

lessons.title: Edging
lessons.text: Lift a knee to tilt the kayak while your body stays upright over it. Edging is the root of turning, bracing and rolling.

lessons.title: The hip snap
lessons.text: A sharp knee lift that rolls the boat back under you. The blade only supports you for a moment; the hips do the work, and the head comes up last.

lessons.title: Where the kayak comes from
lessons.text: Skin-on-frame kayaks were developed over thousands of years by Arctic peoples — Inuit, Yup’ik and Unangan among them — for hunting in cold seas. The traditional watercraft of the Salish Sea is a different boat: the Coast Salish cedar canoe.

lessons.title: Tension the hull
lessons.text: A folding kayak is only as good as its tension. A slack skin wanders and flexes; a tight one tracks true.

lessons.title: Heavy low and central
lessons.text: Water, food and fuel go low and close to the cockpit; light, bulky things go to the ends. A bow-heavy boat ploughs and a stern-heavy boat weathercocks.

lessons.title: The paddle float
lessons.text: A paddle float turns your paddle into an outrigger so you can climb back in alone. You can re-enter without one — it is just much harder.

lessons.title: Carry the essentials
lessons.text: Pump, paddle float, spare paddle, whistle and light, VHF radio, water, food, warm layers and a first-aid kit. You carry them for the day you need them.

lessons.title: Reading the chart
lessons.text: Distances at sea are measured in nautical miles — one minute of latitude, 1,852 metres. The compass rose gives true bearings; the numbers in the water are depths.

lessons.title: Slack water
lessons.text: Between flood and ebb the current pauses. Crossing near slack, or riding a favourable current, is the single biggest decision of the day.

lessons.title: Wind against tide
lessons.text: When the wind blows against the current, waves get shorter and steeper. A moderate breeze over a strong ebb can turn a channel into breaking chop.

lessons.title: Ferry angle
lessons.text: Point partly upstream so the current and your paddling add up to a straight line over the ground. Pick a landmark behind your target and keep the two lined up.

lessons.title: Rest in the eddies
lessons.text: Behind points and in bays the current slows or even flows backwards. Paddlers hop from eddy to eddy to rest and to move against the stream.

lessons.title: Kelp is a harbour
lessons.text: Bull kelp damps waves and slows current. Drape a stalk over your deck and you can rest without drifting.

lessons.title: Tide rips
lessons.text: Where fast water meets a point or shallows it stands up in rough, confused waves. Keep a low brace ready, or go around.

lessons.title: Stay clear of the ferries
lessons.text: Ferries run through San Juan Channel. A kayak is hard to see and must not impede them: cross their lane quickly, at right angles, and as a group.

lessons.title: Give orcas room
lessons.text: In Washington, stay at least 1,000 yards from Southern Resident orcas; never paddle into their path. If whales come near, stop paddling and let them pass.

lessons.title: Let seals rest
lessons.text: Stay at least 100 yards from seals hauled out on rocks. If heads turn toward you or animals shuffle toward the water, you are too close.
About 1 minute to get your breathing under control, about 10 minutes of useful movement to get out, about 1 hour before hypothermia takes consciousness. Act while your hands still work.

lessons.title: Wet exit
lessons.text: Lean forward, pull the grab loop, push the boat away with your hands at your hips and come up beside it. Keep hold of the boat and the paddle.

lessons.title: Paddle-float re-entry
lessons.text: Float on one blade, the other blade under the deck lines behind the cockpit, kick up onto the back deck, hook a leg in, turn and slide down — keeping weight on the float side.

lessons.title: Re-entry without a float
lessons.text: A scramble onto the back deck, belly down and low, is possible in calm water with practice. It is harder in waves — which is why the float earns its place.

lessons.title: Assisted T-rescue
lessons.text: Your partner lifts your bow across their deck to drain it, rights the boat and holds it steady while you climb back in from the side.

lessons.title: The roll
lessons.text: Set up along the side of the boat, sweep the blade out on the surface and snap the hips. The boat comes up first, then the body, then the head.

lessons.title: Pump out
lessons.text: A flooded cockpit makes the boat heavy and tippy. Skirt on, then pump until it is dry.

lessons.title: Camp above the tide
lessons.text: Look for the wrack line of drift logs and seaweed and pitch well above it. Tonight’s high water is higher than this afternoon’s.

lessons.title: Raccoons are clever
lessons.text: Island raccoons open zips and untie knots. Store food in a hard container or a hung bag, never in the tent.

lessons.title: Leave no trace
lessons.text: Camp on durable surfaces, pack out everything you pack in, and leave the island as you found it.

lessons.title: Tide-pool manners
lessons.text: Look with your eyes; touch gently with one wet finger. Never pull an animal off a rock, and turn any rock you lift back exactly as it was.

steps.title: The route
steps.text: Out of the harbour, north up San Juan Channel past Friday Harbor Laboratories and Yellow Island, then across to the north cove on Jones Island. About ten kilometres: two hours at a touring pace, three with a stop on Yellow Island’s lee.

steps.title: Tide and current
steps.text: San Juan Channel floods north-northwest and ebbs south-southeast at up to two knots. Leave on the morning flood and the channel carries you; leave late and you fight the ebb with the afternoon southerly behind it.

steps.title: Traffic
steps.text: The ferries use the harbour entrance and the channel. Cross their lane at right angles, together, and never in front of one: a ferry cannot stop for you.

steps.title: Bail-outs
steps.text: If the wind comes up early: the Friday Harbor Labs shore, then the lee of Yellow Island. Both are landings you can make in a hurry.

steps.title: File it
steps.text: A float plan is only a plan if someone ashore has it: where you are going, when you expect to land, what the boat looks like, and when to call for help if they have not heard from you.

landing.title: The north cove
landing.text: Jones Island. Nose the boat onto the gravel, step out into the shallows and carry it up above the wrack line.

steps.title: Land above the tide
steps.text: Carry the boat up past the wrack line of drift logs and seaweed, and tie it off. Tonight’s high water is higher than this afternoon’s.

steps.title: Pitch on the pad
steps.text: Jones is a marine state park with paddle-in sites on the Cascadia Marine Trail. Use the tent pads and the trail, not the meadow, and leave the firewood on the beach.

steps.title: The raccoons
steps.text: Island raccoons open zips and untie knots. Everything that smells goes in the hard box or a hung bag, never in the tent and never in the boat.

steps.title: Dry out, warm up
steps.text: Out of the drysuit, into dry layers, hot drink before the sun goes. The water is nine degrees and the evening air not much more; the cold catches up with you sitting still.

steps.title: Night in the cove
steps.text: The harbour seals haul out on the point; the Milky Way comes up over Spieden. Tomorrow’s float plan is written tonight, while the tide table is in your head.

steps.title: The route
steps.text: Out of the north cove and west across the top of San Juan Channel, then through Spieden Channel with Spieden Island’s long grass face to starboard and San Juan Island to port. Round Davison Head into the lee of Posey Island, a one-acre park at the mouth of Roche Harbor. About ten kilometres.

steps.title: Tide and current
steps.text: Spieden Channel runs harder than San Juan Channel: the flood sets west through it toward Haro Strait and the ebb east, and off the points it boils. Time the channel for the last of the flood, or for slack, and paddle it in one push — there is nowhere to stop along Spieden.

steps.title: Traffic
steps.text: Roche Harbor is a port of entry with seaplanes and yachts coming and going, and whale-watching boats run Spieden Channel to Haro Strait. Hold your line, stay together, and let the big boats see a group, not a scatter.

steps.title: Bail-outs
steps.text: Spieden Island is private and has no landing. If the channel is more than you want: turn back east for Jones before you are in it, or carry on to the lee of Davison Head and the shore of San Juan Island.

steps.title: File it
steps.text: Update the plan ashore: a new destination, a new landing time. Posey has no water, so the plan says how much you carry and where you will fill up — Roche Harbor, across the channel.

landing.title: Posey Island
landing.text: An acre of rock and madrone with a gravel beach on its sheltered side. Nose in, step out, and lift the boat clear of the tide; there is no room here to leave it on the water line.

steps.title: An island to yourselves
steps.text: Posey is a one-acre marine state park reached only by small boat, with a pair of primitive campsites on the Cascadia Marine Trail. Share it: the next boat in has nowhere else to go.

steps.title: Water you carried
steps.text: There is no drinking water on Posey. What you drink tonight and paddle on tomorrow came in the boat; Roche Harbor, across the channel, is where you fill up.

steps.title: Leave it as found
steps.text: A composting toilet, a fire ring, and nothing else. Pack out everything, keep off the madrones, and let the island’s one acre take the next party as it took you.

steps.title: Dry out, warm up
steps.text: Dry layers before the wind finds you: Posey is open to the west, and the evening breeze comes down Haro Strait off the cold water. Hot drink, then the sun.

steps.title: Night at the mouth of the harbour
steps.text: The sun goes down over Vancouver Island across Haro Strait; the lights of Roche Harbor come on behind you. Listen for the blow of a porpoise, or something larger, in the channel.

legs.title: Posey Island home to Friday Harbor

steps.title: The route
steps.text: The long way home: east through Spieden Channel as it empties, then south down San Juan Channel past Jones Island, Yellow Island and the Labs to the town float at Friday Harbor. About eighteen kilometres, the longest day of the three, and the ebb does the work if you let it.

steps.title: Tide and current
steps.text: This leg is the mirror of the first two. Leave Posey at first light, on the last of the night’s ebb: it runs east through Spieden Channel and south down San Juan Channel, the way you are going, before the southerly gets up. Leave mid-morning and you fight the flood; leave on the afternoon ebb and the wind stands it up against you.

steps.title: Fog
steps.text: First light on cold water often means fog, and it can close in while you are out. The islands go; the compass does not. Hold the bearing you planned, count your strokes, stay within a paddle length of your partner, and show a light. A long blast every two minutes is a vessel under way: stop, listen for where it is, and keep to the edge of the lane until it has passed. It burns off by mid-morning.

steps.title: Traffic
steps.text: The whale-watching fleet works Spieden Channel in the afternoon and the ferries own the harbour entrance. Come into Friday Harbor along the Brown Island side, out of the ferry lane, and cross it only when the dock is clear.

steps.title: Bail-outs
steps.text: Jones Island’s south cove, the lee of Yellow Island, the Friday Harbor Labs shore: the same landings as the way out, in the other order. Nobody has to make it home in one push.

steps.title: Close the plan
steps.text: The float plan ends when you tell the person ashore you have landed. Call before you unpack the boat, not after — a plan that is never closed is a search that starts without you.

landing.title: The town float
landing.text: Friday Harbor. Come alongside the float, out of the ferry’s way, and lift the boat out onto the planks. Three days and two islands behind you.

steps.title: Close the float plan
steps.text: First, before the boat is even out of the water: the call ashore. You are landed, and nobody needs to come looking.

steps.title: Rinse and fold
steps.text: Fresh water through the boat and over the frame, then the skin off and the frame folded back into its bag. A folding kayak that goes away wet comes out of the bag next spring with a smell you will not forget.

steps.title: What you learned
steps.text: You read a tide table and let a channel carry you. You crossed a ferry lane the right way, braced a wave you did not see coming, and left two islands as you found them. That is the whole of sea kayaking; everything after this is practice.

steps.title: The ferry home
steps.text: The boat walks on in its bag, the way it came. Watch the islands go by from the rail and name them: you have paddled under most of them now.

tripDay.label: A July day
tripDay.blurb: Settled summer weather: a light morning, a fresh southerly by mid-afternoon, modest tides.

tripDays.label: A July day
tripDays.blurb: Settled summer weather: a light morning, a fresh southerly by mid-afternoon, modest tides.

tripDays.label: A September day
tripDays.blurb: A spring tide and the first autumn southerly: a stronger stream, twenty knots by early afternoon, and the light gone by seven.

species.blurb: Orcas that hunt marine mammals, travelling quietly in small family groups — and seen here more and more.
facts: They eat seals, sea lions and porpoises, and hunt in near-silence so their prey cannot hear them coming.
Named for Michael Bigg, the scientist who first told orcas apart by their fins and saddle patches.
An adult male’s dorsal fin can stand as tall as a person.
species.where: Anywhere in the islands, all year

species.blurb: The salmon-eating orcas of the Salish Sea — endangered, and never mixing with Bigg’s orcas.
facts: They eat fish, above all Chinook salmon, and travel in three pods: J, K and L.
Listed as endangered in the United States and Canada; fewer than 80 remain.
In Washington, boats must keep at least 1,000 yards away from them.
species.where: Haro Strait and the west side of San Juan Island, when the salmon run

species.blurb: Once hunted out of the Salish Sea, humpbacks have come back in recent decades.
facts: They feed on krill and small schooling fish.
The pattern under each tail fluke is unique and used to identify individuals.
species.where: Open channels and straits, summer and autumn

species.blurb: The most common marine mammal in the Salish Sea.
facts: They haul out on rocks and beaches to rest, especially at low tide.
Pups born in summer are often left alone on shore while the mother feeds — leave them be.

species.blurb: The largest sea lion in the world; big males can weigh around a tonne.
facts: You will often hear them before you see them: a deep roar across the water.
Pale tan to reddish brown, with a broad, blunt, bear-like head.
Unlike seals, sea lions have external ear flaps and walk on their flippers.
species.where: Offshore rocks, mostly autumn to spring

species.blurb: Dark brown, sleek and loud: the barking sea lion of docks and navigation buoys.
facts: Most here are males that come north after the breeding season in California.
Adult males have a raised crest on the top of the head; Steller sea lions do not.
Smaller and darker than the Steller sea lion, which is pale tan with a broad, bear-like face.
species.where: Buoys, docks and rocks, autumn to spring

species.blurb: The otters you see on these shores are river otters, at home in salt water.
facts: They den on land and run easily over rocks — sea otters rarely do.
Look for them porpoising along the shoreline at dawn and dusk.

species.blurb: Rare in the Salish Sea: a sighting here is a real event.
facts: Washington’s sea otters live mostly on the outer coast; only a few have been seen inside the Salish Sea.
They float on their backs and use stones as tools to crack open shellfish.
With no blubber, they keep warm with the densest fur of any animal.
species.where: Very rarely, anywhere; mostly the outer coast

species.blurb: Small, shy and quick — often just a glimpse of a dark back and a soft “puff”.
facts: Among the smallest cetaceans in the world.
They returned to Puget Sound after years of absence.

species.blurb: The smallest baleen whale you will meet here: sleek, quick and usually alone.
facts: Look for a pointed head, a curved dorsal fin that shows at the same moment as the blowhole, and a white band on each flipper.
Its blow is small and hard to see; often the back is the first thing you notice.
Minkes feed on small schooling fish, often over tide rips and banks.
species.where: Open straits and banks, spring to autumn

species.blurb: Black and white, very fast, and famous for its “rooster tail” of spray.
facts: At speed it throws a cone of spray off its back, so you often see more splash than porpoise.
One of the fastest small cetaceans, it loves to ride the bow waves of boats.
Fewer are seen in Puget Sound now than in past decades.

species.blurb: The San Juan Islands hold one of the densest nesting populations in the lower 48 states.
facts: They build huge nests in tall shoreline trees and reuse them for years.
Their call is a surprisingly thin, high whistle.

species.blurb: The fastest animal on Earth in its hunting dive.
facts: In a stoop it can pass 300 km/h (about 200 mph).
Wiped out across much of North America by the pesticide DDT, it recovered and came off the US endangered list in 1999.
Cliffs and seabird colonies make the islands good hunting ground.

species.blurb: A blue-grey bird with a shaggy crest and a loud, rattling call.
facts: It hovers or watches from a perch, then plunges headfirst for small fish.
Unusually for birds, the female is the more colourful: she has a rusty band across her belly.
It nests in a burrow dug into an earth bank.

species.blurb: A black seabird with white wing patches — and startling red feet and mouth.
facts: They nest in crevices in rocky cliffs and bluffs.
They dive and swim underwater using their wings.

species.blurb: A relative of the puffins, named for the pale horn on its bill in breeding season.
facts: They carry fish back to their burrows in the evening.
Protection Island in the Strait of Juan de Fuca hosts a large colony.

species.blurb: Stands motionless in the shallows, then strikes.
facts: Eelgrass beds are rich hunting grounds for small fish.
They nest together in colonies high in trees.

species.blurb: An all-black shorebird with a bright orange-red bill and a loud, piping call.
facts: It pries limpets and mussels off rocks with its chisel bill.
It lives only on rocky shores.
species.where: Rocky shores at the tide line

species.blurb: A slim, glossy black diver that nests on sheer cliff ledges.
facts: It nests on narrower ledges than other cormorants; in the Salish Sea more and more pairs now nest on bridges.
It swims underwater with its feet, then stands with its wings held open to dry.
In breeding season it has white patches on its flanks and a red face. Give rookeries a wide berth: a flushed bird can leave its eggs to gulls.
species.where: Cliff ledges; rookeries from April to August

species.blurb: The largest octopus species in the world.
facts: It can change colour and skin texture in a moment.
It lives only a few years, dens under rocks, and leaves a midden of crab shells at the door.
species.where: Rocky reefs; rarely, the lowest tide pools

species.blurb: Purple or orange, clinging to rocks at the low-tide line.
facts: A classic keystone species: by eating mussels it keeps room on the rocks for many other animals.
Sea star wasting disease killed huge numbers from 2013; populations are still recovering.

species.blurb: Once common, now critically endangered: the biggest, fastest sea star of these waters.
facts: It can have up to 24 arms and grow about a metre across.
Sea star wasting disease killed about nine in ten of them from 2013; the species is now listed as critically endangered.
It eats sea urchins and so helps protect kelp forests. If you see one, report it.
species.where: Rocky reefs below the low-tide line; rarely in the lowest pools

species.blurb: Its green colour comes from algae living inside it.
facts: It catches crabs, mussels and small fish that fall into its tentacles.

species.blurb: A sea slug in electric orange and blue.
facts: It eats hydroids and keeps their stinging cells for its own defence.

species.blurb: A translucent bell drifting beneath the hull.
facts: The four horseshoe shapes you can see through the bell are its reproductive organs.

species.blurb: The largest jelly in these waters, trailing a curtain of fine tentacles.
facts: Its bell is red-brown to yellow, and its tentacles can stretch for metres.
It stings, and even a broken-off tentacle can. Keep your hands out of the water around it.

species.blurb: A pale bell with a yolk-yellow centre. It really does look like a fried egg.
facts: It eats other jellies, especially moon jellies.
Small crabs and fish sometimes ride along beneath its bell.
species.where: Open water, late summer and autumn

species.blurb: A clear jelly that glows at its rim, and changed biology.
facts: Its green glow comes from green fluorescent protein, now used in labs around the world to light up living cells.
Osamu Shimomura collected hundreds of thousands of them at Friday Harbor Laboratories from 1961, and shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery.
species.where: Friday Harbor and calm bays, summer

species.blurb: On summer nights every paddle stroke can leave a trail of blue sparks.
facts: Single-celled plankton flash when the water around them is disturbed.
species.where: Dark, calm bays on summer nights

species.blurb: A brown alga that grows from the seabed to the surface in a single season.
facts: It can grow many centimetres in a day, buoyed by a gas-filled float.
Kelp forests shelter young fish — and they have declined in parts of the Salish Sea.

species.blurb: A single long golden-brown blade with ruffled edges.
facts: It grows from a holdfast on rocks, just below the low-tide line.
Dried, it tastes faintly sweet. It is eaten, and farmed, in the Pacific Northwest.

species.blurb: Bright green sheets, thin enough to see through.
facts: Each sheet is only two cells thick.
It grows fast where nutrients are high, and can pile up on beaches in summer.

species.blurb: A red seaweed covered in little bumps. It feels like a towel.
facts: It grows in the lowest tide pools and shallow water below.
Its blades are rich in carrageenan, a thickener used in foods.

species.blurb: Not a seaweed but a flowering plant that grows underwater.
facts: Eelgrass meadows are nurseries for herring and young salmon.

species.blurb: Red bark that peels in curls, leaning out over the water from dry rocky bluffs.
facts: Madrona in Washington, arbutus in British Columbia, madrone further south: three names for the same tree.
A broadleaf evergreen: it keeps its glossy leaves all year and sheds its bark instead.

species.blurb: The tall conifer of every island skyline.
facts: Despite its name it is not a true fir.
Its cones have three-pointed bracts poking out between the scales.

species.blurb: Soft, rot-resistant and fragrant — the tree from which Coast Salish canoes are carved.
facts: It grows best in moist, shaded ground.
Its drooping branches and stringy bark make it easy to tell from the firs around it.

species.blurb: The only native oak of these islands, standing in open, grassy meadows.
facts: Garry oak meadows are among the most endangered ecosystems in the region.
